asDecan.p: Jupiter rules the first ten degrees of Gemini in the Golden Dawn's order, where the sign is at its freshest, and your Sun is somewhere in there. It's an awkward match, to be honest. Jupiter's home sign is Sagittarius, directly across the zodiac, which puts it in detriment here, working against the grain. Jupiter wants one big belief to stand on. Mercury rules Gemini and wants the next fact, the counter-argument, the footnote. Put Jupiter inside that and it does what it always does, makes everything bigger, the options and the doubts together. The Nine, Mars's slice, is sharper and more personal, an argument you keep having with someone who isn't there. The Ten, the Sun's, is about bringing a thing to its end. Yours is the widest of the three and the least decided. Have a look at the picture, a woman among the swords with open ground behind her. The Lovers is still your Sun card. This one belongs to your ten degrees of it.

You've got fourteen tabs open on your phone and at least three of them are about the same decision. Choosing a sofa, or a school for a kid, or a new phone plan, you'll read every review, ask four friends, and come back to the first option a fortnight later. At a family dinner you're the one who can argue any side, and you'll sometimes swap sides halfway through just to see if it holds up. A Sunday with nothing planned can go entirely on deciding what to do with it, the beach or the markets or finally sorting the spare room, and by four o'clock it's too late for any of them. You're also very good company on a long drive, since you know something about almost everything and will happily talk about any of it for three hours.

You're very good at spotting other people's cages. A friend says they can't possibly ask for flexible hours, and you're the one who asks whether anyone has actually said no or whether they've just assumed it. You'll read the tenancy agreement a mate is panicking about and find the clause that lets them out early. Jupiter struggles in Gemini, and I think that's partly why this works. You've had so much practice arguing with your own assumptions that other people's are easy to see. You're also good at the generous second opinion. When two people at work have fallen out, you can usually find the version of events where nobody's the villain, and once you say it out loud the whole office tends to settle.

Where it shows is your calendar. Jupiter is generous and Gemini says yes to anything interesting, so you agree to the book club, the side project, helping your cousin move, and the short course you found at midnight. Three weeks later you feel boxed in and resentful, and it's hard to admit that nobody signed you up for any of it but you. There's a quieter one too. You can tell the story of being stuck so well, so funny and so detailed, that telling it starts to stand in for doing anything about it. Your friends have been hearing about the job you're about to leave for two years. They enjoy the story. That's a problem, because it means nobody ever pushes you.

When something goes wrong, a redundancy or a health scare in the family or a friend who's stopped speaking to you, your first move is to find out everything. You read, you ring people, you ask the same question three different ways. That helps for about two days. By the end of the week you've often gone still. The email's unanswered, the appointment isn't booked, and you're sleeping badly because your head keeps running the cases at night. The people around you tend to get either a long anxious commentary or silence, and both are hard to help with. What actually helps is shrinking it. Pick one question you can get a real answer to within a few days and go and get it. Walking helps too, oddly, a long one, with the phone left in your pocket.

The Lovers is a card about choosing, and this slice of Gemini finds choosing hard, so the chart's having a small joke at your expense. Mostly it shows up after the choice is made. You're with someone, it's fine, it's good even, and some part of you keeps a quiet file of other lives you could be living. You don't act on it. You just never quite close the question, and a partner can feel that even when they can't name it. People with this Sun are often drawn to someone with a big, simple view of life, the sort who says 'we're doing this' and means it. That can be lovely, since it's the long view Jupiter can't quite hold in you. It can also mean they end up making every big call, the suburb, the kids, and years later you're sore about it and can't say why.

Gemini gives you range and Jupiter gives you appetite, so you do well wherever breadth is the job, teaching, research, journalism, sales, any role that pays you to learn something fast and explain it to someone else. The snag tends to be in the fine print of your own situation. I've seen a lot of people in this part of Gemini assume there's a rule stopping them from moving sideways, asking for training or changing teams, and never check. Ask HR the actual question. Ask your manager. Surprisingly often the answer is yes and nobody thought to say so. You also work best alongside one colleague who's good at finishing things, and if you've found that person, keep hold of them.

At twenty this part of Gemini is usually great fun and all over the place. Two degrees started, a band, three part-time jobs, and a lot of worry about picking the wrong life, which seems to be the main fear at that age. There's often a stretch in the twenties of feeling stuck while surrounded by options, which is a confusing thing to explain to anyone. By the mid-thirties most people with this Sun have worked out that putting off a choice is a choice too, and they start committing to fewer things and finding they lose less than they feared. The fifties tend to be kind to this Sun. The worrying gets smaller, Jupiter's long view seems to arrive late, and a lot of them become the person everyone rings to talk something through.

Next time you feel stuck with something, a job, a lease, a commitment you made in a weak moment, write the rule that's keeping you there on a scrap of paper in one plain sentence. 'I can't leave before the contract ends.' 'I have to go to every one of these.' Then find out, from the person or the document, whether that rule is real. Do it for one rule only. Sometimes it turns out softer than you thought, and sometimes it doesn't, and then at least you know what you're actually up against.
